newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Diplomacy presses Zaire foes into fresh talks.
newsitem.headline: Diplomacy presses Zaire foes into fresh talks.

text.p: Diplomatic pressure has pushed Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila to agree fresh talks and political manoeuvering intensified on both sides.

Mobutu returned to Kinshasa on Saturday, where his supporters in parliament filled the vacant post of Speaker -- a potential interim leader to whom Mobutu could give power, depriving Kabila of the clean handover he demands.
Kabila said he had agreed to meet Mobutu for talks, but ruled out calling off his military drive which has reached to less than 200 km (125 miles) from the teeming capital of five million.
"No one has officially asked me to stop my offensive. We shall continue," Kabila said in a television interview.

South Africa's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki said the two would meet face-to-face on board a South African ship. A first ship-borne meeting between the two, hosted by South Africa's Nelson Mandela, ended inconclusively a week ago.

A constitutional successor for Mobutu emerged from Zaire's parliament, where lawmakers voted Roman Catholic Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo into the key post of Speaker -- who takes over in the event of Mobutu's death or incapacity.
"He is not an alternative to either President Mobutu or Kabila," Christophe Lutundula, second deputy speaker of parliament, told Reuters.
"We are hoping he will play a role as a national mediator and will persuade all sides to agree on a way of safeguarding the democratic process in Zaire."
But radical opposition deputies boycotted the vote and it was unclear whether a necessary quorum was in place.
Mobutu and several other French-speaking African leaders, meeting on Thursday, proposed a stronger role for parliament in solving Zaire's crisis and called for a new Speaker.
But rebels rejected the proposal as "nonsense" and said Mobutu must hand over power directly to Kabila or be driven from Kinshasa by advancing fighters.
Rebel "foreign minister" Bizima Karaha accused the Central African presidents of "playing games and trying to protect Mobutu. But we cannot be fooled".
Monsengwo has not said whether he will take the job.

Mobutu, 66, has used political cunning to dominate the mineral-rich country at the heart of Africa for more than three decades until prostate cancer and the rebellion, launched in October, loosened his hold.
In seven months, the rebels, initially a small force fighting for ethnic Tutsis, have won control of around three quarters of the vast country.
Mobutu's most enduring Western ally, France, welcomed Monsengwo's election, saying it could help an orderly transfer of power in Kinshasa.
A foreign ministry spokesman said his election appeared to facilitate "an orderly transition (in Zaire) within an institutional and legal framework".

The United States, which backed Mobutu in the Cold War as an ally against Soviet communist expansion, has said any new government would "most likely" be headed by Kabila in light of his military victories.
Companies looking for rights to exploit Zaire's vast mineral wealth are already at Kabila's doorstep. One has already signed a $1 billion deal with the rebels.
